key_insight: At reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces, small polarons move far more slowly than in bulk because surface geometry removes many favorable hopping paths and confines motion mainly to limited in-plane routes.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous or defect-rich rutile TiO2 can show much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, which matters for optimizing catalysts, photovoltaic electrodes, and energy-storage devices.
method: Machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics extended from bulk to oxide surfaces
Nanosecond-scale finite-temperature dynamics on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110)
Analyze polaron hopping pathways and vacancy-induced charge trapping
evidence_signal: The study uses several nanoseconds of simulation across multiple temperatures and finds surface polaron mobility is suppressed by several orders of magnitude relative to bulk.
watch_item: The results are specific to one reduced oxide surface and still depend on the quality and transferability of the trained machine-learning model.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
